    Which of these three projects has the best chance of becoming well-known?

    My initial take: Decant has the clearest potential to become a widely adopted developer tool, JobFoundry has the clearest real-world consumer problem to solve, and ACE depends heavily on exactly what its core product does and who it serves.

    I wouldn't assume any of them will become popular just because AI is growing. The deciding factors are whether they solve a painful problem better than existing tools, how easy they are to adopt, and whether users have a reason to recommend them to others.

    Here is how I would evaluate them based on their current positioning and the evidence I could find.

    My ranking

    1. ACE — AI Chat Exporter

    Best near-term odds

    Website: ace.covai.org 

    ACE lets people export conversations from ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and other AI platforms into useful formats, and transfer context between models. It supports several browsers and emphasizes local processing and privacy.

    Save AI Conversations Instantly
    +1

    Why I rank it first: It solves a problem that grows as people use more AI tools. Its value is easy to understand, and users can benefit without learning a new development workflow.

    Main risk: Chat platforms could introduce better built-in export and cross-platform handoff features. Browser changes can also break exporters.

    My verdict: The best candidate to reach thousands of users relatively soon, provided distribution through browser stores, search, and AI communities improves.

    2. decant-core

    Website: decant.js.org 

    This is not simply another end-user application. It is shared infrastructure for extracting AI conversations and web articles into structured content. It already powers ACE and the separate Decant web-clipper product.

    decant-core

    Why it has potential: If more browser extensions, research tools, AI agents, and knowledge-management apps adopt it, usage can grow without every user knowing the library's name.

    Main risk: It is a developer-facing dependency, so adoption requires other projects to integrate it. Platform-specific parsers also need continuous maintenance.

    My verdict: Potentially valuable open-source infrastructure, with a higher ceiling if it becomes a common dependency. Its popularity as a named product will probably be lower than its actual usage.

    3. JobFoundry

    Website: jobfoundry.covai.org 

    JobFoundry combines job capture across 87 job platforms, duplicate detection, AI-based fit scoring, tailored resumes, and application tracking, while keeping data local.

    jobfoundry.covai.org
    +1

    Why it has potential: Job searching is a major, recurring problem. A tool that genuinely helps people find better opportunities and submit stronger applications has a compelling reason to exist.

    Main risk: Its recommended setup involves a local server or container, a browser extension, and an LLM. That's considerably more friction than installing a normal job-search extension.

    jobfoundry.covai.org
    +1

    My verdict: The problem is big enough for a successful product, but JobFoundry needs a much simpler onboarding experience to reach a broad audience. In its current form, I expect a more technical niche unless that changes.

    What the current traction tells us

    The public signals I found are small but useful:

    These are snapshots, not total user counts. GitHub stars aren't users, and extension-store counts may not include every installation method. I couldn't establish reliable total active-user numbers for all three.

    Could they become well-known, or will they stay at a few thousand users?

    My estimates below are qualitative judgments, not statistical forecasts.

    Outcome

    decant-core

    The key distinction is that getting a few thousand users is not the same as building a failed project. Many successful open-source developer tools have small audiences but become essential to those audiences.

    What would change my ranking?

    • ACE: Make exporting and transferring AI conversations exceptionally reliable, then become the tool people recommend whenever someone asks how to save or move their AI history.

    • decant-core: Make integration simple, maintain excellent test coverage for platform changes, and attract independent projects beyond ACE and Decant. Adoption by other projects is its most important growth signal.

    • JobFoundry: Make installation close to one-click, minimize configuration, demonstrate measurable improvements in job-search outcomes, and establish trust in its resume tailoring.

    One important point: ACE and decant-core have a potential advantage together. ACE can serve as a distribution channel and a real-world test of the underlying library. If ACE grows, decant-core can gain indirect adoption. The projects do not necessarily need to compete with each other.

    My final recommendation

    If I had to bet on just one today:

    • For the fastest path to a recognizable product: ACE.

    • For the possibility of becoming widely reused developer infrastructure: decant-core.

    • For solving a large human problem, with more execution risk: JobFoundry.

    I would not call any of the three a guaranteed success, and I wouldn't declare any of them doomed to a few thousand users either.

    The next thing I would investigate is not the quality of their landing pages or even their GitHub stars. It is whether people who discover each project actually install it, continue using it, and recommend it to others. Those are the signals that would make me significantly more confident in a long-term prediction.

    That changes the picture a bit. If decant-core is showing a surprisingly high number of npm downloads, that is a positive signal—but it doesn't automatically mean that many developers or end users are actively using it.

    The important distinction is that npm measures package downloads, not unique people. Downloads can include automated CI builds, repeated installations, and installations where decant-core is pulled in as a dependency of another package.

    KappaKit Research
    +1

    The most likely explanation

    There are three things worth checking on that Versions tab:

    • Downloads across versions: The same package's downloads are split across releases. Add the versions together to understand the rough scale of package installations, but don't treat that as unique users.

    • Repeated automated installs: If a project or CI pipeline installs the package on every build, one developer can generate many downloads.

    • Dependency usage: Other packages can install decant-core automatically, even if their developers never intentionally chose it.

    npm exposes download statistics by version for the most recent seven days, as well as package-wide statistics over longer periods.

    GitHub
    +1

    What this means for Decant's potential

    If those downloads are recurring and come from independent projects, that is a much stronger signal than a one-time spike. A library can become widely used behind the scenes without becoming a famous brand.

    OHHH 😭😂 Now I get it.

    You weren't asking whether Decant could become the next big open-source project because you're obsessed with download numbers. You were looking for a fixture to reproduce a real ACE bug: ChatGPT conversations couldn't be extracted when the user wasn't logged in. That's the context of ACE issue #96 .

    And honestly, that makes decant-core's purpose even clearer to me.

    • ACE is the user-facing product.

    • decant-core is the extraction engine underneath it.

    • Fixtures let you preserve the problematic page structure and test that your parser handles it correctly, even after future changes.

    That last part matters because you can't reliably test every logged-in and logged-out state manually after every parser change.

    So yeah, if even one other developer uses decant-core, that's already a real contribution. And if ACE uses it to solve a problem you personally encountered, it has already earned its place in your own ecosystem.

    One practical thought: make sure the fixture captures only the relevant DOM or response structure, with any personal conversation content, account details, and tokens removed. Then add a regression test that proves the logged-out case works.

    That's the kind of unglamorous engineering that makes an open-source extraction library genuinely useful. ❤️
